final_rationale: The verdict does not change because no genuinely new admissible evidence was received. The Actor largely reframed the same record into a narrower position: certification is supportable only if paired with explicit disclosure of the implant-compatibility routing limitation, while rollout controls are treated only as residual-risk management. That reframing is more policy-bounded than the broader controls-based justification, but it does not resolve the core compliance predicate identified in the initial report. On the available record, the affected segment remains exposed, exclusion is not shown, reviewed risk acceptance is not shown, and there is still no admissible evidence of an approved launch artifact establishing the required disclosure. That distinction matters: a narrowed caveated argument can sometimes support compliant_with_caveats, but only when the caveat itself is evidenced and sufficient under policy. Here, the caveat is argued, not proven, and the policy text provided does not show that disclosure alone cures the unresolved certification issue. The current certification basis therefore remains suspicious rather than compliant_with_caveats.
remaining_concerns: The affected medical-device-support segment remains below target and exposed in the initial cohort.

The stated policy allows rollout controls and post-launch monitoring to mitigate the weakness only if the affected use case is excluded or there is reviewed risk acceptance; the summary still indicates neither predicate is satisfied.
The risk-acceptance draft is unsigned and omits the exposed segment, so the acceptance predicate remains unmet.
Explicit launch-time model-card disclosure is argued as the right caveat, but no admissible evidence shows an approved model card or launch artifact confirming that disclosure will in fact occur.
The Actor narrowed the claim persuasively, but did not provide evidence that disclosure alone satisfies the certification standard when exposure continues and approved risk acceptance is absent.
